nameStory: The name 'columbine' comes from the Latin 'columba,' meaning dove, because the five spurred petals were thought to resemble a cluster of doves drinking from a fountain. The spurs are the backward-pointing tubes that hold nectar, and if you use your imagination, they do look like little dove heads dipping down for a sip! This charming flower is also known as 'granny's bonnet' because the entire bloom resembles an old-fashioned frilly cap.
description: Common columbine is a graceful perennial flower that forms bushy clumps and can grow up to 3 feet tall. This European native has become widely naturalized in New England gardens and wild spaces. The distinctive flowers are the star of the show - they're typically blue or purple, about 2 inches across, and have an unmistakable shape with five petals that extend backward into hollow spurs. The plant produces delicate, compound leaves that are divided into rounded leaflets, giving the whole plant an airy, cottage garden appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled blooms with distinctive backward-pointing spurs (hollow tubes) that feel papery to the touch. Flowers are typically blue, purple, or sometimes white, measuring about 2 inches across and dangling gracefully from branching stems.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, blue-green compound leaves divided into three sets of rounded, lobed leaflets. The leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, with a delicate texture that bruises easily when handled roughly.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms bushy clumps up to 3 feet tall with multiple flowering stems rising from a basal rosette. The overall appearance is graceful and airy, not dense or compact like many other perennials.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops clusters of upright, pointed seed pods that split open when ripe to release small black seeds. The dried pods make a subtle rattling sound when shaken and persist into fall.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Branching flower stems are smooth and somewhat hollow, with a crisp snap when broken. They often have a slight reddish tinge and feel sturdy despite their delicate appearance.

habitat: Common columbine thrives in partially shaded areas with rich, well-draining soil, often found in woodland edges, cottage gardens, and naturalized areas. In New England, you'll commonly spot it in semi-wild spaces around old homesteads, along stone walls, and in mixed perennial borders where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers cooler, moister conditions than many flowers and often grows alongside ferns, wild ginger, and other woodland plants.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as distinctive blue-green compound leaves in early spring, forming attractive mounds even before flowering begins. The plant is easily recognizable by its characteristic leaf shape and color.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from May through June, when the unmistakable spurred flowers appear in abundance. After flowering, the upright seed pods develop and can be observed forming throughout mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen and split open, releasing seeds, while the foliage often takes on yellowish tones before dying back. The dried stems and empty seed pods may persist, rattling in autumn breezes.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, leaving no above-ground trace until spring growth begins again. Look for the location by noting where dried stems were in fall.

funFact: This innocent-looking garden favorite was once considered so powerful that it symbolized the Holy Spirit in medieval Christian art, yet Shakespeare used it as a symbol of adultery in Hamlet - talk about mixed messages! The plant contains compounds that are actually mildly toxic to humans, which might explain why our ancestors viewed it with such complex reverence and suspicion.
confusionNotes: The distinctive spurred flowers make common columbine nearly impossible to confuse with any other plant when in bloom. However, the foliage might be mistaken for wild ginger or some buttercup family members, but columbine's leaves have a more blue-green color and feel more delicate and papery to the touch.
contextualKnowledge: While beautiful and widely grown, common columbine contains alkaloids that are toxic to humans and animals if consumed in large quantities, so it was traditionally used very cautiously as an herbal remedy. Despite its common name, this species is actually European in origin and has naturalized so successfully in New England that many people assume it's native - it's been here since colonial times and growing in gardens for over 800 years!
compareHints: Common columbine can be distinguished from our native red columbine by its blue or purple flowers (versus bright red and yellow) and its more robust, bushier growth habit. Red columbine is typically found in wilder, rockier settings and has a more delicate, woodland appearance, while common columbine thrives in garden settings and forms denser clumps. The spurs on common columbine are also typically shorter and more curved compared to the longer, straighter spurs of red columbine.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red columbine is the only native columbine species in New England, making it easy to distinguish from the escaped garden columbines you might occasionally find.
Blue columbine stands out from its eastern cousin, red columbine, primarily by color - blue and white versus red and yellow.
Dark columbine is easily separated from our native red columbine by its dark purple-black flowers versus red and yellow ones.
Golden columbine stands out from other columbines by its pure yellow flowers and extra-long spurs.
